title: How to Spot Fake Sneakers — A Buyer's Guide
excerpt: Fakes are getting better, but they still slip up in the same places. Here's the checklist we use before any pair goes out the door.
content:
Fake sneakers are everywhere, and the good ones are getting scary close to the real thing. The bad news: you can't always tell from a single photo. The good news: fakes still slip up in the same handful of places. Learn them and you'll save yourself money and embarrassment.

1. Start with the seller, not the shoe

Before you look at a single stitch, look at who's selling. Do they have a real shop or pickup point? Do they answer questions about size and stock without dodging? Can you inspect the pair before you pay, or at least get a proper return path? A seller who hides behind "DM for price" and vanishes when you ask for extra photos is telling you everything.

2. If the price feels too good, it is

Every model has a realistic price range. A pair selling at half of what everyone else charges is not a lucky insider deal. Either it's fake, it's stolen, or it's a trap. Sales and clearance are real, but they come with honest labels like "end of line", not mystery.

3. Check the box and the label

  • Style code: The code on the box label should match the code on the tag inside the shoe. Type it into a search engine. It should pull up the exact model and colourway.
  • Print quality: Blurry fonts, crooked barcodes or spelling mistakes on the label are a red flag.
  • Size consistency: The size on the box, the tongue tag and the insole should all agree.

4. Look at the build, not the logo

Everyone checks the logo first, so fakers work hardest there. Look at the boring stuff instead:

  • Stitching: Straight, even, tight. Loose threads, double stitches and wandering lines mean a rushed factory.
  • Glue: A little cement here and there happens on real pairs too, but fat glue stains around the midsole edge are common on fakes.
  • Shape: Real pairs sit symmetrical. Put both shoes side by side and check the toe box, the heel curve and how they stand on a flat surface.
  • Materials: Cheap synthetic feels plasticky and stiff. A harsh chemical smell out of the box is a warning sign.

5. Check the inside

Pull out the insole. Real pairs usually have clean, neat construction underneath, with tidy stitching and clear internal labels. Fakes often leave the inside rough because nobody expects you to look. Check the tongue label and the size tag too. Fonts should be crisp and evenly spaced.

6. Weight and feel

If you've handled the real thing before, you'll notice the difference immediately. Performance shoes like running and basketball pairs are engineered for weight and cushioning. A fake usually feels heavier, stiffer or oddly hollow. The sole should flex where your foot flexes, not somewhere random.

7. Ask for proof

Before you pay for anything online, ask for:

  • A photo of the box label and the tag inside the shoe
  • The insole pulled out
  • The outsole, close up
  • A short video of the actual pair, not a stock photo

A genuine seller will do all of that without attitude. If they get annoyed, walk.

The safest way to buy is the simplest one: pick up in person, check the pair in your hands, and pay once you're happy.

A quick note on honest flaws

Real sneakers can have small factory flaws too, like a stray thread or a bit of glue. One tiny flaw isn't proof of a fake. What matters is the pattern: wrong label, wrong materials, rough inside, weird price and a shady seller, all together.

Buy from people you can reach, ask questions, and trust your gut. If something feels off, it probably is.

title: Running Shoes vs Lifestyle Sneakers — What's the Actual Difference?
excerpt: They can look alike on the shelf, but they're built for very different jobs. Here's how to pick the right one and stop wrecking your knees.
content:
Walk into any sneaker shop and a running shoe and a lifestyle sneaker can look like cousins. Same laces, same sole, same fresh colours. But they're built for completely different jobs, and wearing the wrong one for the wrong job costs you comfort, money and sometimes your joints.

What running shoes are built for

A running shoe is engineered around one movement: your foot hitting the ground over and over, thousands of times per outing. Everything is designed to manage that impact and keep you moving forward.

  • Cushioning: Thick midsole foam absorbs impact and returns some energy so each step feels less harsh.
  • Weight: Lightweight materials so your legs aren't hauling bricks by kilometre five.
  • Breathable uppers: Mesh that lets heat out, because running feet get hot fast.
  • Sole shape: A rockered or gently curved sole helps you roll forward from heel to toe.
  • Grip: Rubber pods or patterns designed for tarmac, tracks or trails.

What lifestyle sneakers are built for

Lifestyle sneakers, sometimes called casual or fashion sneakers, are built to look good and hold up to everyday wear. Comfort matters, but style leads.

  • Flatter, sturdier soles: Less foam, more structure. They feel stable when you're standing and walking around.
  • Durable materials: Leather, canvas, suede and synthetics that keep their shape and clean up well.
  • Design first: Colourways, silhouettes and details that go with jeans, shorts and everything in between.

The big differences at a glance

  • Impact protection: Running wins by a mile.
  • Everyday style: Lifestyle wins, though modern running shoes have closed the gap a lot.
  • Weight: Running shoes are usually lighter.
  • Longevity of looks: Lifestyle pairs often hold their shape longer when you're not pounding the road.

Can you run in lifestyle sneakers?

For a short jog to catch a matatu, sure. For training, no. Flat, firm soles don't absorb repeated impact well, and that's how you end up with sore shins, tired feet and worse. If you're running more than the occasional sprint, get an actual running shoe.

Can you wear running shoes every day?

Absolutely, and plenty of people do. Running shoes are comfortable for long days on your feet, especially if you're walking a lot around town. The trade-off is that soft foam wears down faster with constant use, so if you run in them, keep a second pair for daily wear.

Where each one goes wrong

Running shoes worn as full-time fashion pairs wear out quickly, because soft foam compresses with every step and the outsole rubber is thin to save weight. Lifestyle sneakers pushed into serious training let you down the other way: too firm, too heavy, not enough support when the kilometres pile up. Match the shoe to the job and both types last far longer.

How to choose

Ask yourself one question: what will I do in these shoes most of the time?

  • Running or gym cardio: Go for a proper running shoe.
  • Long days walking around the city: A cushioned running shoe or a comfort-first walking shoe.
  • Hanging out, work, going out: Lifestyle sneakers.
  • Mix of everything: Get one of each and rotate. Your feet, and your shoes, will last longer.

Not sure which side of the fence you're on? Tell us what you'll be doing in them and we'll point you to the right pair.

title: How to Clean Your Sneakers and Keep Them Looking Fresh
excerpt: You don't need fancy products. A soft brush, mild soap and a bit of patience will bring most pairs back from the dead.
content:
A fresh pair doesn't stay fresh by accident. Nairobi dust, muddy rain-season puddles and crowded matatu floors will humble any pair. The good news is that cleaning sneakers properly is easy and cheap. You don't need special kits. You need the right steps, in the right order.

What you'll need

  • A soft-bristle brush (an old toothbrush works for small spots)
  • A microfibre cloth or clean towel
  • Mild soap or laundry liquid
  • A bowl of lukewarm water
  • Old newspaper or paper towels

Step 1: Strip them down

Take out the laces and the insoles. Laces go in a separate wash, and insoles get cleaned on their own so they can dry properly. Knock the shoes together outside to shake loose dirt.

Step 2: Dry brush first

Before any water touches the shoe, brush off the loose dust and dried mud with your soft brush. If you skip this, you just turn dust into mud and rub it into the fabric.

Step 3: Mix your cleaner

Add a few drops of mild soap to a bowl of lukewarm water. Not hot, because heat can weaken the glue that holds your shoe together. Skip bleach and harsh detergents, since they can yellow and damage materials.

Step 4: Scrub gently

Dip your brush, shake off the extra water and scrub the upper in small circles. Work from the top down. Use your cloth to wipe away the suds as you go. Mesh and knit uppers need a light touch, since rough scrubbing can fuzz or snag them.

Step 5: Do the midsole and outsole

The midsole is where scuffs and stains live. Give it a slightly firmer scrub with the same soapy mix. Check the outsole grooves and pick out any stones or dirt stuck in the tread, because that keeps your grip working properly.

Step 6: Wipe, don't soak

Wipe everything down with a clean damp cloth to remove soap. Never dunk your shoes in a bucket. Soaking loosens glue and leaves water trapped inside, which leads to smell and damage.

Step 7: Dry the right way

Stuff the shoes with newspaper or paper towels to hold the shape and soak up moisture. Change the paper after an hour or two. Let them air dry somewhere shaded with good airflow. Do not use direct sun, a heater or a dryer. Heat warps soles, cracks materials and can make white midsoles yellow.

Special cases

  • Suede: Use a dry suede brush or eraser and skip water where you can.
  • White soles: A paste of baking soda and water, applied gently and wiped off, helps lift stains. Test it on a small spot first.
  • Laces: Hand wash in soapy water or put them in a small mesh bag for a gentle machine cycle.

Please don't put them in the washing machine

We know it's tempting. Don't. The tumbling and heat can break down cushioning and glue, and your pair will never feel the same.

Give your pair a quick wipe after heavy wear and a proper clean every few weeks. Small effort now means you keep wearing them for far longer.

title: Finding Your True Size — Why Sneaker Sizing Isn't Always What You Think
excerpt: Same number, different fit. Here's how to measure your feet properly and stop guessing every time you order.
content:
You wear a 42 in one shoe and a 43 in another. That's not you changing. That's sneaker sizing being a bit of a mess. Different brands, different shapes and different materials all mean the number on the box is only a starting point. Here's how to get it right, especially when you're ordering without trying on.

Why sizes don't match

There's no single global standard that every brand follows. Each one builds shoes around its own "last", the foot-shaped mould the shoe is made on. A narrower last, a thicker toe cap or a sock-style upper can all change how a shoe fits, even at the same number. Running shoes, basketball shoes and casual sneakers also tend to fit differently from each other.

How to measure your feet at home

  1. Measure in the evening. Feet swell a little through the day, so this gives you your real size.
  2. Stand on a sheet of paper against a wall, with your heel touching the wall.
  3. Mark the tip of your longest toe. It isn't always the big one.
  4. Measure from the wall to the mark in centimetres.
  5. Do both feet. Most people have one bigger than the other, so go with the larger.

Then compare that length to the size chart for the shoe you want. If you fall between two sizes, read on.

How much room do you need?

For most shoes, leave about a thumb's width between your longest toe and the front of the shoe. Your toes should wiggle freely, your heel shouldn't slip and the middle of your foot should feel held, not squeezed.

  • Running shoes: Feet slide forward and swell on longer runs, so a little extra room is normal. Many runners go up half a size or a full size from their casual shoe.
  • Lifestyle sneakers: These are usually closer to your true size. A snug fit that softens with wear is normal.
  • Basketball and court shoes: You want a locked-in feel for quick changes of direction, so don't go too big.

Width matters too

If a shoe feels tight on the sides but the length is right, the shoe is probably too narrow for you, not too short. Going up a size just makes it sloppy at the heel. Look for models with a roomier toe box instead.

Socks count

Try shoes with the socks you'll actually wear. A thick training sock can change the fit more than you'd think.

When you're ordering online

  • Check the size chart for the exact model, not just the brand.
  • Read reviews for comments like "runs small" or "runs narrow".
  • Message the seller with your foot length and ask for advice. A good seller will tell you honestly.
  • If a pair is available for pickup, try it on before you pay.
Rule of thumb: when two sizes both feel almost right, choose the one that lets your toes move.

Still unsure? Send us your foot length in centimetres and the pair you're eyeing, and we'll tell you what we'd go for.

title: Best Sneakers for Nairobi's Streets — Comfort Meets Style
excerpt: Potholes, dust, matatu stages and rainy season. Here's what to look for in a pair that survives the city and still looks good.
content:
Nairobi is hard on shoes. You've got long walks from the stage, uneven pavements, surprise puddles when the rains hit and dust the rest of the year. The right sneakers make all of that easier. The wrong ones leave you with sore feet and a ruined pair. Here's what actually matters.

1. Grip you can trust

Wet tarmac, smooth paving tiles and muddy paths can all get slippery. Look for an outsole with deep, well-spaced tread. A rubber sole with a decent pattern beats a flat, smooth one every time, especially in the long rains from March to May and the short rains later in the year.

2. Cushioning for long days

If you're on your feet from the CBD to Westlands, cushioning isn't a luxury. A midsole with foam that absorbs impact keeps your feet and knees from feeling it by evening. Cushioned running shoes make great everyday pairs for exactly this reason.

3. Breathability

Warm afternoons and packed public transport get sweaty. Mesh uppers let your feet breathe and dry quickly if they get wet. Fully sealed synthetic pairs can trap heat and smell.

4. Colours that forgive dust

All-white is fresh, but it takes work. Darker colours, greys, and two-tone designs hide dust and marks much better between cleans. If you love white, keep a brush and cloth close by.

5. Easy on and off

Slip-on and quick-lace styles are a blessing when you're rushing out of the house or taking them off at someone's door. Just make sure the heel still holds your foot securely.

Pick by what your week looks like

  • The daily commuter: Cushioned, breathable, grippy. A road running shoe or urban walking shoe fits perfectly.
  • The weekend runner: A proper running shoe with a firmer, responsive feel, plus a second casual pair for the rest of the week.
  • Court regular: Padel, tennis or basketball shoes built for side-to-side movement, worn for the court and kept clean for it.
  • The style-first crowd: Lifestyle sneakers with a clean silhouette that works with jeans, chinos and shorts.

Don't ignore fit

A stunning pair in the wrong size is a bad pair. Aim for a thumb's width of space at the toe and a snug, locked-in heel. If you're unsure of your size, call or message before ordering.

Rainy-season rules

When the rains hit, walk around puddles where you can, since standing water is deeper than it looks. If your shoes get soaked, don't leave them wet in a bag. Take the insoles out, stuff the shoes with paper and let them dry slowly in a shaded, airy spot. Mesh pairs dry fastest, which is one more reason to keep a breathable pair in your line-up for the wet months.

Rotate, if you can

Wearing the same pair every single day wears out the cushioning quicker and leaves no time for the shoe to dry out. Two pairs in rotation last longer than one pair worked to death.

The best sneaker for Nairobi is the one that feels good at 8 a.m., still feels good at 8 p.m., and doesn't make you panic when it rains. Start there, then pick your colour.

title: Sneaker Care 101 — Storage, Cleaning and Longevity Tips
excerpt: Good kicks aren't cheap. Here's how to store them, look after them and squeeze every last kilometre out of a pair.
content:
You paid for a good pair, so make it last. Sneaker care isn't about being precious. It's about a few simple habits that stop your shoes from breaking down early. Here's the full routine, from storage to when it's time to say goodbye.

Rotate your pairs

If you can, don't wear the same shoes two days in a row. Foam cushioning needs about a day to bounce back, and shoes need time to dry out completely. Even a simple rotation of two pairs makes a real difference to how long each one lasts.

Let them breathe after wear

When you get home, loosen the laces, pull the tongue forward and take the insoles out if they're damp. Leave the shoes somewhere with airflow instead of tossing them in a cupboard sweaty. Trapped moisture is what causes smell and breaks down the materials from the inside.

Keep the shape

Stuff the toe box with paper or use shoe trees, especially for leather and canvas pairs. This stops creasing and keeps the shoe from collapsing while it's stored.

Store them smart

  • Cool and dry: Avoid damp corners, direct sunlight and the boot of a hot car. Heat and humidity age glue and rubber fast.
  • Not sealed and damp: If you use boxes, make sure the shoes are fully dry first. Toss in a silica gel sachet to control moisture.
  • Not squashed: Don't pile heavy things on top. Shoes stored side by side keep their shape better than a crushed stack.

Clean little and often

A quick wipe with a damp cloth after dusty days is far easier than a full deep clean later. Dirt left in the fabric wears it down. For a proper clean, use a soft brush, mild soap and lukewarm water, and dry the shoes slowly in the shade. Skip the washing machine and the sun.

Protect them before trouble hits

A protective spray suited to your shoe's material helps repel water and stains, especially on canvas and suede. Reapply every so often, and always test on a small area first.

Look after the small parts

  • Laces: Wash them separately. Replace frayed ones before they snap.
  • Insoles: Swap them out when they flatten or start to smell no matter what you do.
  • Soles: Pick stones out of the tread and check for uneven wear, which can hint at how you walk or run.

Deal with smell early

Sprinkle baking soda inside overnight and shake it out the next day, or leave the shoes with a silica sachet. Wearing proper socks helps more than any spray.

Know when they're done

Running shoes lose their cushioning long before they look worn out. A common rule of thumb is to replace them somewhere between 500 and 800 kilometres, sooner if you're heavier or run on rough ground. Warning signs include new aches in your feet or shins, visibly flattened foam and worn-through tread.

For casual pairs, look for cracked soles, separating glue or uppers that have lost their support. Small repairs, like re-gluing an edge, are worth doing early. Left alone, they turn into a bin job.

Treat your pair right and they'll return the favour, on the road, on the court and everywhere in between.
